dct_description_sm:
This dataset identifies areas of Canada where whooping cranes (Grus americana) are known to have occurred. 

The whooping crane is protected under the Migratory Birds Convention Act and has been listed as endangered under the Species at Risk Act since 2003. The Aransas-Wood Buffalo population (AWBP) is the only remaining wild, self-sustaining population of the species, and the only one that occurs in Canada. The AWBP spends roughly half of its annual cycle in Canada, migrating through Alberta, Saskatchewan and occasionally Manitoba to breeding areas in and around Wood Buffalo National Park in northern Alberta and the Northwest Territories. 

The dataset draws on two independent sources. The first is satellite tracking of individually marked cranes, carried out by the Whooping Crane Tracking Partnership, a collaboration among Environment and Climate Change Canada, Parks Canada, the United States Fish and Wildlife Service and the United States Geological Survey. Between December 2009 and December 2025, 182 cranes were captured and fitted with GPS (Global Positioning System) tracking devices to monitor their movement, behavior and survival during all aspects of their annual cycle, yielding more than 13.5 million recorded locations. Recording frequency varied among devices and across years. Transmitters were programmed to collect GPS locations at variable frequencies over the duration of the project, ranging from 4–5 locations per day for devices deployed prior to 2015 to intervals of 1 second to 30 minutes for those deployed after 2016. This schedule allows for detailed information on diurnal and nocturnal habitat use and on migratory behavior in spring and fall. The second source is 2,908 confirmed whooping crane nests recorded during aerial surveys of the breeding range in and around Wood Buffalo National Park between 1966 and 2025.

To build a single dataset, locations recorded within Canada were summarized using the Nested Hexagon Framework (Houts et al. 2023), a standardized grid of nested hexagonal cells covering North America that allows information from different sources to be combined at a common scale. This dataset uses the largest cell size in that framework, approximately 343 square kilometers. Each cell is flagged for the presence of tracking locations and, separately, for the presence of confirmed nests; cells containing neither are not included. The result is a single map layer of 2,298 cells, supplied as geographic information system files in GeoPackage, GDB, and KMZ formats, which can be opened in common mapping and analysis software. Every cell contains tracking locations, and 32 also contain confirmed nests. The dataset covers parts of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, Nunavut and British Columbia, corresponding to the Canadian portion of the population's migration corridor and its breeding range.

Season of use is not recorded in this dataset, so it should be interpreted alongside the timing of whooping crane movements. Migration through the Prairie provinces occurs between April 2 and May 22 in spring, and between September 4 and November 3 in fall. Subadult birds may spend summers in central and southern SK and AB within the migration corridor. Cranes may therefore be present in the Prairie provinces at any time between April 2 and November 3, and on the breeding range between April 15 and November 1.

Several limitations apply to the dataset, as presented. As only a portion of the population carries a tracking device at any one time, this dataset is not a complete map of the species' distribution in Canada, and the absence of data in a cell does not mean that cranes are absent. Cells record presence only: they carry no information on how many birds used an area, over how many days or years, in which season, or how intensively, and a cell visited once cannot be distinguished from one visited many thousands of times. Tracking locations include birds both on the ground and in flight. This data form part of an ongoing monitoring and research program and should be treated as preliminary.

Finer scale tracking data may be requested under a data sharing agreement to support regulatory needs such as impact assessments. In most cases, finer-scale NHF summaries provide the appropriate level of detail, though raw individual records with movement and life-history attributes can be considered when justified based on project objectives. Please direct inquiries to the Habitat and Data Management Unit, Canadian Wildlife Service, Prairie Region.

We thank partners who supported whooping crane tracking (International Crane Foundation, Parks Canada, United States Fish and Wildlife Service, United States Geological Survey, Wilder Institute) and nest monitoring (Parks Canada).

References:  Houts, Michael, D. Fross, M.T. Connor, C. Bishop. 2023. Nested Hexagon Framework and Landscape Summary Database. Kansas Biological Survey and Center for Ecological Research, University of Kansas. https://kars.geoplatform.ku.edu/pages/nhf-lsdb
dct_title_s: Whooping Crane occupancy and nesting areas in Canada, 1966-2025
